topic: Day 2 · Determining Stroke Aetiology — The TOAST Work-up
speakerAffiliation: Virtual Teaching Hospital · Stroke Prevention Clinic
speakerBio: Believes a stroke without a diagnosed mechanism is just a rehearsal for the next one.
lectureHTML:
🎯 The case on the table

Your patient's acute stroke is treated and stable — but unless you find why it happened, you are just waiting for the next one. Two strokes with identical scans can have completely different causes and therefore completely different prevention. Aetiology is the hinge between the acute phase and a lifetime of protection.

1 · Why aetiology drives everything

Secondary prevention is only as good as the cause you identify — an antiplatelet does nothing for an untreated AF, and anticoagulation does not fix a critical carotid. Find the mechanism, then match the prevention.

2 · The TOAST classification

TOAST categoryCluePrevention
Large-artery atherosclerosisCarotid/intracranial stenosis; cortical infarctAntiplatelet + statin; carotid revascularisation if symptomatic stenosis
CardioembolismAtrial fibrillation, LV thrombus, endocarditis, prosthetic valve, PFO; multiple territoriesAnticoagulation (AF); treat the source
Small-vessel (lacunar)Deep small infarct; hypertension, diabetesAggressive BP/risk-factor control, antiplatelet
Other determinedDissection, vasculitis, thrombophilia, PFO with paradoxical embolismCause-specific
Undetermined (cryptogenic / ESUS)No cause found despite work-upProlonged monitoring for occult AF

3 · The work-up toolkit

  • Vessels: carotid Doppler / CTA / MRA — find operable stenosis and dissection.
  • Heart: ECG, telemetry, and prolonged/ambulatory monitoring (24 h → 7-day → implantable loop recorder) to catch paroxysmal AF; echocardiography (TTE, TOE for cardiac source/PFO/endocarditis).
  • Blood: glucose/HbA1c, lipids; targeted thrombophilia/vasculitis screens in the young or atypical.

4 · ESUS and the hunt for occult AF

💡 Cryptogenic ≠ no cause — it means "keep looking"

Embolic stroke of undetermined source (ESUS) often hides paroxysmal atrial fibrillation that a single ECG misses. CRYSTAL-AF and EMBRACE showed that prolonged monitoring (implantable loop recorders, extended Holter) detects far more AF than routine testing — and finding it changes the patient from an antiplatelet to anticoagulation. Empirical anticoagulation for ESUS without AF did not beat aspirin (NAVIGATE-ESUS/RE-SPECT ESUS), so the answer is to find the AF, not to guess.

☠️ M&M — the AF that a single ECG missed

A patient with a cortical stroke had one normal ECG, was labelled cryptogenic and discharged on aspirin. Months later he had a second, disabling stroke; a loop recorder then revealed paroxysmal AF he had had all along. Lesson: one ECG does not exclude paroxysmal AF. In embolic-pattern strokes, pursue prolonged cardiac monitoring — because the difference between aspirin and anticoagulation is the difference between the first stroke and the second.

5 · Take-home

  • Match prevention to mechanism — TOAST is the map.
  • Image the carotids and hunt for AF — the two most actionable causes.
  • ESUS = keep looking; prolonged monitoring finds occult AF (CRYSTAL-AF/EMBRACE).
  • Do not empirically anticoagulate ESUS without documented AF.

moderatorQs.q: Why does finding the aetiology matter so much?
moderatorQs.answerHTML: Because prevention is mechanism-specific. An antiplatelet does nothing for untreated atrial fibrillation, and anticoagulation does not fix a critical carotid stenosis. The TOAST categories — large-artery, cardioembolic, small-vessel, other, and undetermined — each map to a different prevention strategy, so the work-up is what converts an acute event into effective lifelong protection.

moderatorQs.q: What does the aetiology work-up actually involve?
moderatorQs.answerHTML: Three axes: vessels (carotid Doppler/CTA/MRA to find operable stenosis or dissection), heart (ECG, telemetry, prolonged monitoring for paroxysmal AF, and echocardiography including TOE for cardiac source or PFO), and blood (glucose/HbA1c, lipids, with targeted thrombophilia/vasculitis screens in the young or atypical). The two highest-yield actionable findings are carotid stenosis and AF.

moderatorQs.q: How hard should we look for occult atrial fibrillation?
moderatorQs.answerHTML: Hard — a single ECG misses paroxysmal AF. CRYSTAL-AF and EMBRACE showed prolonged monitoring (extended Holter, implantable loop recorders) detects far more AF, and finding it switches the patient from an antiplatelet to anticoagulation. Importantly, empirically anticoagulating ESUS without documented AF did not beat aspirin, so the goal is to find the AF, not to guess.

audienceQs.answerHTML: Embolic Stroke of Undetermined Source — a non-lacunar, embolic-appearing infarct with no identified cardioembolic or large-artery cause after a standard work-up. It is a signal to keep looking, especially for paroxysmal AF with prolonged monitoring, rather than a final diagnosis. Most of the yield comes from cardiac rhythm monitoring.

audienceQs.q: When do I request a transoesophageal echo rather than transthoracic?
audienceQs.answerHTML: When you need better views of the left atrium/appendage, interatrial septum (PFO/ASD), aortic arch, and valves — for example in a young cryptogenic stroke, suspected endocarditis, or to characterise a PFO for possible closure. TTE is the first-line screen; TOE is the higher-resolution follow-up when a cardioembolic or septal source is suspected.
